Permanent from a Determinant

VP ≠ VNPParityPermutations
Game: Put minus signs on some of the letters so that the determinant's products all come out positive, turning the determinant into the permanent.
How to play: Click a letter to give it a minus sign, and click again to take it off. For 3 × 3, get as many of the six products positive as you can.

    A bigger determinant that does it: Grenet’s matrix

    Look for the math

    The determinant is easy to compute and the permanent seems hard, yet they differ only in signs. So can a determinant be made to compute the permanent? This is the form in which Leslie Valiant posed the question behind VP ≠ VNP.

    Changing signs: only for 2 × 2

    For 2 × 2, putting a minus on b gives det [[a, −b], [c, d]] = ad + bc, the permanent. George Pólya asked in 1913 whether signs can do this for larger squares. For 3 × 3 they cannot. Each letter appears in exactly two of the six products, so flipping its sign flips two products at once. The number of minus products starts odd (three) and stays odd. The logic test tried all 512 sign patterns: the best is 5 positive out of 6. Gábor Szegő proved that no signs work for any size from 3 up.

    A bigger square can do it

    Make a vertex for every set of columns. From a set of size k, draw an arrow to each set with one more column j, labelled with the entry in row k + 1, column j. Each route from the empty set to the full set picks one entry per row in different columns: one rook product, and every one appears once. Join the full set back to the empty set and put a 1 on the diagonal for every other set. The determinant of that matrix of size 2ⁿ − 1 is exactly the permanent. This is Bruno Grenet's construction (2011). For 3 × 3 it is the 7 × 7 matrix above, and Alper, Bogart and Velasco showed that 7 is the smallest size possible. The test checked the construction for sizes 2, 3 and 4.

    The real question

    Call the smallest determinant that computes the n × n permanent its determinantal complexity, dc(n). Grenet shows dc(n) ≤ 2ⁿ − 1. The best lower bound known is about n²/2 (Mignon and Ressayre, 2004). Valiant conjectured that dc(n) grows faster than any power of n. That is the determinant-versus-permanent form of VP ≠ VNP: easy determinants cannot disguise the hard permanent without becoming enormous. Gil Fried's article reports a proof of VP ≠ VNP announced in 2026; this page explains the question and does not check that claim.

    Try the 2 × 2 first. Then on 3 × 3, see which single letter, when flipped, turns the most products positive.
